Catechetical School
kat-eh-KET-ih-kul skool
noun phrase (the school of Alexandria)
From “catechetical” (of instruction, Greek katecheo); chiefly the catechetical school of Alexandria, the early centre of Christian learning under Pantaenus, Clement, and Origen.

📖 Biblical Definition

The catechetical school most famously names the school of Alexandria, the early and influential centre of Christian instruction and scholarship that flourished from the late second century under Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen. Founded to instruct converts and catechumens in the faith, it grew into a centre of advanced theological learning where Christianity engaged the philosophy, science, and literature of the Hellenistic world. The dictionary weighs the school with discrimination. Its commendable aim was real: the careful instruction of believers in the faith and the training of teachers, in the spirit of the apostolic charge to instruct, that men might know the certainty of the things wherein they were catechized, and to train up the young in the way they should go. The defence of the faith before a learned pagan world was a worthy labour. But the dictionary names the school's besetting fault: it pioneered and propagated the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture, treating the literal sense as a husk to be discarded for hidden spiritual meanings, and it married Christian doctrine too closely to Neoplatonic philosophy—errors that reached their height in Origen, whose speculations (on the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration, and the subordination of the Son) departed gravely from the faith. Against the school of Alexandria stood the school of Antioch, with its sounder literal-historical method, which the Reformers' own exegesis followed. The dictionary honours the catechetical school's zeal for learning and instruction while naming its allegorizing and philosophical entanglement as the seedbed of much later error, holding that the church's schools must instruct the young in sound doctrine and the plain sense of the Word, no prophecy of Scripture being of any private interpretation.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early centre of Christian learning at Alexandria (Pantaenus, Clement, Origen); honoured for its zeal to instruct and engage the learned world, yet named the seedbed of allegorical exegesis and Neoplatonic entanglement, against the sounder school of Antioch.

CATECHETICAL SCHOOL, noun phrase. [Greek katecheo, to instruct.] Chiefly the school of Alexandria.

Flourished from the late 2nd century under Pantaenus, Clement, and Origen.

Founded to instruct converts; grew into a centre of theological learning.

Pioneered the allegorical method and married doctrine to Neoplatonic philosophy.

Opposed by the sounder literal-historical school of Antioch.

📖 Key Scripture

Lu 1:4 — "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."

Ac 18:25 — "This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John."

2 Pe 1:20 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation."

Pr 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The school of Alexandria pioneered allegorical exegesis and married doctrine to Neoplatonic philosophy, errors that reached their height in Origen's grave speculations.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the catechetical school's commendable aim—the careful instruction of converts in the faith and the training of teachers, that men might know the certainty of the things wherein they were catechized. To instruct the young in sound doctrine and to defend the faith before a learned pagan world is honourable labour, and Alexandria gathered real gifts to that end.

Yet the dictionary names the school's besetting faults. It pioneered and propagated the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture, discarding the literal sense for hidden meanings, and it married Christian doctrine too closely to Neoplatonic philosophy. These errors reached their height in Origen, whose speculations on the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration, and the subordination of the Son departed gravely from the faith. Against Alexandria stood the school of Antioch, with its sounder literal-historical exegesis, which the Reformers' own interpretation followed. The dictionary holds that the church's schools must instruct in sound doctrine and the plain sense of the Word, remembering that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation—honouring the zeal of Alexandria while refusing the method that became the seedbed of much later error.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek katecheo (to instruct by word of mouth), whence “catechetical”; the Alexandrian school of instruction that became a centre of theological learning.

Katecheo, Greek, to instruct, the root of “catechetical.”

The school of Alexandria, founded to instruct converts and catechumens.

Led successively by Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen.

Pioneer of the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture.

Opposed by the literal-historical school of Antioch.

Usage

"The teacher honoured the catechetical school's zeal to instruct while naming its allegorizing."

"He traced Origen's grave speculations to the school's marriage of doctrine and philosophy."

"She held that the church's schools must teach the plain sense of the Word, not private interpretation."
